newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Aide doubts Israel's Netanyahu will be indicted.
newsitem.headline: Aide doubts Israel's Netanyahu will be indicted.

text.p: An aide to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday he did not believe the state prosecutor would implement a police recommendation that Netanyahu be charged with fraud and breach of trust.

Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh admitted if there were charges they could result in Netanyahu's "dismissal", but said the police recommendation was not well-enough founded "to change the course of history".
Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak rejected calls for the prime minister's resignation.
"The prime minister has no intention of going now to elections or to resign or to suspend himself," Bazak told Israel Radio. "The prime minister is confident in his innocence. We are all sure of it."

Naveh told the radio he was quoting from a police letter to the prosecutor: "We are aware of the problematics of presenting an indictment on an issue that is so complicated and sensitive based on one central witness who could be seized on and presented by the defence as untrustworthy and perhaps even an interested party."

Naveh then said: "And I want to ask, do you present an indictment against the prime minister in Israel, something that could in effect bring about the dismissal of the prime minister in Israel, pervert the wishes of the voters of only a year ago, change the course of the history of the State of Israel on a basis like this? My answer to this question is negative.
"You do not dismiss the prime minister of Israel, you do not contradict the voter's wishes, you do not change the course of history on this basis."
Police said on Wednesday Netanyahu should be charged with fraud and breach of trust in an influence-peddling scandal. They said the recommendation was based on one witness's testimony.
The news dealt a crippling although not necessarily fatal political blow to the right-wing leader, analysts said.
Israel's state prosecutor can ignore the recommendation to put Netanyahu on trial for his short-lived appointment of political crony Roni Bar-On as attorney general in January.

A minister close to Netanyahu said the Likud party leader might have to call an election if there was a decision to prosecute. Asked what would happen if prosecutors pressed charges, Health Minister Yehoshua Matza told Israel Radio in English: "Perhaps it will be to go back to elections."
News of the possible charges came during a visit by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross who is trying to salvage Israel-PLO peace talks. Ross and Palestinian officials called the news an internal Israeli affair.
Netanyahu was elected with a slim 30,000 vote-majority over Labour's Shimon Peres last May. Peres called the news an "earthquake".

Police have been looking into the Bar-On appointment since January. Channel One television had alleged a Netanyahu ally on trial for corruption, politician Aryeh Deri, pushed Bar-On for the job in the hope of winning a plea bargain.
Deri in return had promised his Shas party's support for Netanyahu's deal with the Palestinians to redeploy in the West Bank town of Hebron, the television report said.
Bar-On quit hours after being appointed amid criticism he was professionally unfit for the job.
